title: Opioids & Pain Pharmacology
summary: Opioid receptors, analgesic mechanisms, overdose reversal and multimodal pain control.

lessons.title: Pain Pathways

levels.kid:
When you touch something hot, special nerve endings in your skin called **pain sensors** notice the danger. They send a fast message up nerves to your spinal cord, then up to your brain. Your brain says "Ouch!" and you pull your hand away.

Pain is like a smoke alarm. It's annoying, but it keeps you safe.

Your body also has a **volume knob** for pain. The brain can send messages down to turn pain louder or quieter. Rubbing a bump helps a little because it turns the volume down. Pain medicines work at different spots along this path.
levels.hs:
**Pain** starts with **nociceptors**, free nerve endings that detect harmful heat, pressure or chemicals. Two fiber types carry the signal:
- **Aδ fibers:** thin, myelinated, fast. Sharp, well-localized "first pain".
- **C fibers:** unmyelinated, slow. Dull, burning, aching "second pain".

The signal enters the **dorsal horn** of the spinal cord, where the fibers release **glutamate** and **substance P**. Second neurons cross to the other side and ascend in the **spinothalamic tract** to the thalamus, then the somatosensory cortex (where and how strong) and limbic areas like the cingulate cortex (how unpleasant).

**Modulation:**
- **Gate control:** touch fibers activate spinal inhibitory neurons that "close the gate" on pain, which is why rubbing helps.
- **Descending control:** the brainstem (periaqueductal gray and rostral ventromedial medulla) sends serotonin, noradrenaline and **endorphin** signals down to dampen pain.

**Types of pain:** nociceptive (tissue injury), inflammatory, **neuropathic** (damage to nerves themselves) and nociplastic (altered pain processing, e.g., fibromyalgia).

**Drug targets:** NSAIDs reduce prostaglandins at the injury site; local anesthetics block nerve conduction; opioids act in spinal cord and brain; some antidepressants boost descending inhibition.
levels.college:
**Transduction:** nociceptor channels include **TRPV1** (heat, capsaicin, protons), **TRPA1** (irritants, cold), **TRPM8** (cold), **ASICs** (acid), **Piezo2** (mechanical, mainly touch) and **P2X3** (ATP). Voltage-gated sodium channels **Nav1.7, Nav1.8 and Nav1.9** are enriched in nociceptors.

**Peripheral sensitization:** inflammatory mediators (PGE2, bradykinin, NGF, histamine, cytokines) lower activation thresholds via PKA/PKC phosphorylation of TRPV1 and Nav1.8, producing **hyperalgesia** and **allodynia** at the injury site. **Neurogenic inflammation:** peptidergic C fibers release CGRP and substance P, causing vasodilation and edema (the target of CGRP drugs in migraine).

**Dorsal horn:** Aδ fibers end in laminae I and V, C fibers in laminae I and II (substantia gelatinosa). Projection neurons ascend via the **anterolateral system**: lateral spinothalamic (to VPL thalamus → S1, sensory-discriminative) and spinoreticular/spinoparabrachial pathways (to medial thalamus, ACC, insula, amygdala, affective-motivational).

**Central sensitization:** repetitive C-fiber input relieves the Mg2+ block of **NMDA receptors**, causing **wind-up** and long-term potentiation; spinal glia amplify signaling.

**Descending modulation:** PAG → RVM (ON and OFF cells) → dorsal horn. Noradrenergic input from the locus coeruleus acts on spinal **α2 receptors** (inhibitory); serotonergic input can inhibit or facilitate.

**Pharmacological map:** COX inhibitors (periphery and spinal cord), acetaminophen (central), local anesthetics (Nav channels), opioids (presynaptic and postsynaptic dorsal horn, PAG, RVM), gabapentinoids (α2δ on presynaptic calcium channels), SNRIs and TCAs (descending inhibition), α2 agonists, and **suzetrigine**, a selective **Nav1.8 blocker** approved in 2025 for acute pain.
levels.phd:
**Human genetics validates targets.** Loss-of-function mutations in **SCN9A** (Nav1.7) cause congenital insensitivity to pain, while gain-of-function mutations cause inherited erythromelalgia and paroxysmal extreme pain disorder. This seemed a perfect analgesic target, yet selective Nav1.7 blockers largely failed. Explanations include insufficient target engagement at axonal terminals and the discovery that Nav1.7-null humans and mice have **upregulated endogenous opioid signaling** (naloxone restores pain in null individuals), meaning channel loss alters a whole network rather than simply blocking spikes. Nav1.8 inhibition (suzetrigine) succeeded clinically in acute pain where Nav1.7 did not, with efficacy in neuropathic pain still under study.

**Spinal disinhibition.** After nerve injury, microglia release **BDNF** (downstream of P2X4 activation), which downregulates the potassium-chloride cotransporter **KCC2** in lamina I neurons. Intracellular chloride rises, so GABA and glycine become less inhibitory or even excitatory, allowing Aβ touch input to access nociceptive circuits (mechanical allodynia). Sex differences exist: in male rodents this pathway is microglia-dependent, while females rely more on T-cell mechanisms, a caution for translation.

**Predictive processing and the pain matrix.** Imaging shows no single "pain center"; the salience network (ACC, insula) responds to unexpected stimuli generally. Placebo analgesia engages prefrontal-PAG circuits and endogenous opioids (partially naloxone-reversible), and nocebo involves cholecystokinin. Expectation modulates spinal dorsal horn activity directly, shown with spinal fMRI.

**Chronification.** Longitudinal imaging of back pain implicates corticostriatal (medial prefrontal-nucleus accumbens) connectivity as predicting transition from acute to chronic pain, framing chronic pain partly as a learning process. This supports multimodal treatment beyond nociceptor-directed drugs.
levels.expert:
**Classify the pain before choosing the drug.** Nociceptive pain (fracture, surgery) responds to NSAIDs, acetaminophen, local anesthetics and opioids. Neuropathic pain (burning, shooting, electric, with sensory loss) responds better to gabapentinoids, SNRIs and TCAs than to opioids. Nociplastic pain (widespread, with fatigue, poor sleep) needs exercise, sleep and psychological approaches, with SNRIs or TCAs as helpers. Mixed pain is common: a radiculopathy has both inflammatory and neuropathic elements.

**Multimodal analgesia** combines drugs acting at different points of the pathway so each can be used at lower intensity with fewer side effects: acetaminophen plus NSAID plus regional anesthesia, with opioids reserved for breakthrough pain. This is central to enhanced recovery protocols.

**Examination clues:** dermatomal sensory loss suggests radiculopathy; stocking-glove loss suggests polyneuropathy; allodynia and hyperalgesia indicate sensitization; autonomic changes (color, temperature, sweating) with disproportionate pain suggest complex regional pain syndrome.

**Red flags** that change management: fever, weight loss, history of cancer, new neurological deficit, saddle anesthesia or urinary retention (cauda equina), and pain in a patient on anticoagulants (hematoma).

**Neurosurgical pain procedures** map onto the pathway:
- **Microvascular decompression** for trigeminal neuralgia removes vascular compression of the nerve root entry zone.
- **Spinal cord stimulation** (dorsal columns) applies gate-control logic for failed back surgery syndrome and CRPS.
- **Dorsal root entry zone lesioning** for brachial plexus avulsion pain.
- **Cordotomy** (spinothalamic tract interruption) for refractory unilateral cancer pain.
- **Intrathecal drug pumps** deliver opioids or ziconotide, an N-type calcium channel blocker.

**Pitfall:** escalating opioids for pain that is neuropathic or nociplastic usually adds harm without benefit.

keyPoints: Aδ fibers: fast, sharp pain; C fibers: slow, burning pain.
Dorsal horn → spinothalamic tract (crosses in the cord) → thalamus → S1, ACC, insula.
Peripheral sensitization (PGE2, bradykinin, NGF) and central sensitization (NMDA wind-up).
Descending control: PAG → RVM → dorsal horn; noradrenaline acts on spinal α2 receptors.
Pain types: nociceptive, inflammatory, neuropathic, nociplastic.
Drug targets span the path: COX, Nav channels (incl. Nav1.8 blocker suzetrigine), opioid receptors, α2δ, NMDA.

lessons.title: Opioid Receptors and Agonists

levels.kid:
Your body makes its own pain-calming chemicals called **endorphins**. They fit into special locks on nerve cells called **opioid receptors**, like keys in locks. When a key turns, the pain message gets quieter.

Opioid medicines, like **morphine**, are keys that fit those same locks. Doctors use them for very bad pain, like after surgery or a broken bone.

But these keys also slow down breathing and make people sleepy and constipated. They can be very dangerous if not used exactly as a doctor says, so only doctors decide who gets them.
levels.hs:
**Opioid receptors** are G protein-coupled receptors found in the brain, spinal cord and gut. Three main types:
- **μ (mu):** most painkilling effect, plus **respiratory depression**, sedation, constipation, **pinpoint pupils** (miosis), nausea, cough suppression and reward effects that create addiction risk.
- **κ (kappa):** spinal pain relief, sedation, unpleasant mood (dysphoria) and increased urination.
- **δ (delta):** pain relief and mood effects.

**Natural opioids made by the body:** endorphins, enkephalins and dynorphins.

**Opioid agonists** used in medicine include **morphine**, **codeine**, **oxycodone**, **hydromorphone**, **fentanyl** and **methadone**. They differ in strength, how fast they act and how long they last.

**How they block pain:** activated receptors close calcium channels on the sending neuron (less neurotransmitter release) and open potassium channels on the receiving neuron (making it harder to fire).

**Tolerance** (needing more for the same effect) develops to pain relief and breathing depression, but **not** to constipation or pinpoint pupils. **Physical dependence** means stopping suddenly causes withdrawal. Because of these risks, opioids are used for the shortest time needed, often combined with non-opioid painkillers.
levels.college:
**Receptor signaling:** μ (MOR, OPRM1), κ (KOR) and δ (DOR) couple to **Gi/o**:
- Inhibit adenylyl cyclase (↓cAMP).
- Presynaptic: Gβγ closes **N- and P/Q-type calcium channels** → less glutamate, substance P release.
- Postsynaptic: Gβγ opens **GIRK** potassium channels → hyperpolarization.
- β-arrestin recruitment drives receptor desensitization and internalization.
The related **NOP** (nociceptin) receptor is insensitive to naloxone.

**Endogenous ligands:** β-endorphin (from POMC, μ), enkephalins (from proenkephalin, δ>μ), dynorphins (from prodynorphin, κ).

**Key agonists:**
- **Morphine:** glucuronidated to **M6G** (active, accumulates in renal failure) and **M3G** (neuroexcitatory). Histamine release (itch, hypotension).
- **Codeine:** prodrug activated by **CYP2D6** to morphine. Ultrarapid metabolizers risk toxicity; poor metabolizers get little analgesia. Contraindicated in children under 12.
- **Tramadol:** weak μ agonist (via CYP2D6 metabolite) plus serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibition; seizures, serotonin syndrome, hypoglycemia.
- **Oxycodone, hydromorphone:** semisynthetic; hydromorphone preferred in renal impairment over morphine.
- **Fentanyl, sufentanil, remifentanil:** highly lipophilic phenylpiperidines; rapid onset; chest wall rigidity with rapid IV use. Remifentanil is ester-hydrolyzed by plasma esterases.
- **Methadone:** μ agonist plus NMDA antagonist; long, variable half-life; **QT prolongation**; many CYP interactions.
- **Meperidine:** metabolite normeperidine causes seizures; serotonin syndrome with MAOIs; largely avoided.

**Effects to which tolerance does not develop:** miosis and constipation. **Opioid-induced hyperalgesia** can develop with prolonged exposure. Opioids also suppress the HPA and gonadal axes long term.
levels.phd:
**Biased agonism, rise and fall.** Mice lacking β-arrestin-2 showed enhanced morphine analgesia with less respiratory depression and constipation, suggesting G-protein-biased μ agonists could separate benefit from harm. Oliceridine and PZM21 were developed on this premise. Subsequent work challenged it: independent β-arrestin-2 knockout lines and mice with phosphorylation-deficient MORs (which cannot recruit arrestin) still showed full respiratory depression. Reanalysis indicated that apparent bias often reflected **low intrinsic efficacy** (partial agonism) and assay amplification differences. Oliceridine's clinical respiratory safety margin over morphine was modest. The lesson: system bias and partial agonism can masquerade as ligand bias.

**Respiratory depression circuitry.** MORs on neurons of the **preBötzinger complex** (inspiratory rhythm generator) and the **Kölliker-Fuse/parabrachial** complex mediate rate depression; deleting MOR from these sites largely prevents it. Opioids also blunt chemoreceptor responses to CO2 and hypoxia and impair arousal, which is why sleep and co-sedatives magnify risk.

**Tolerance mechanisms.** Acute desensitization involves GRK-mediated phosphorylation of the MOR C-terminal tail and arrestin binding; long-term tolerance involves adenylyl cyclase superactivation (cAMP overshoot underlying withdrawal in locus coeruleus neurons), NMDA-dependent plasticity, and glial activation. Morphine, a poor internalizer, paradoxically produces more tolerance than efficacious internalizing agonists in some models (the RAVE hypothesis), though this remains debated.

**Structural pharmacology.** Crystal and cryo-EM structures of MOR with agonists, antagonists and Gi reveal a conserved aspartate (D147) salt bridge with the protonated amine, and agonist-specific rearrangements of transmembrane helix 6. Structure-based docking of millions of virtual compounds discovered novel scaffolds, illustrating modern GPCR drug discovery.

**Peripheral opioid analgesia.** Inflammation upregulates MOR transport to peripheral terminals and opens the perineurial barrier, explaining local opioid benefit in inflamed joints.
levels.expert:
**Choosing an opioid (clinical reasoning, no recipes):**
- **Renal failure:** avoid morphine (M6G and M3G accumulate, causing prolonged sedation, myoclonus, seizures) and codeine; fentanyl or hydromorphone with care, since fentanyl clearance is largely hepatic.
- **Hepatic failure:** reduced clearance and increased oral bioavailability of high-extraction opioids; encephalopathy risk.
- **Elderly or frail:** start lower, titrate slowly, monitor sedation before breathing changes.
- **Pharmacogenomics:** CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers turn codeine and tramadol into active metabolites quickly; pediatric deaths after tonsillectomy led to regulatory contraindications.
- **Methadone:** obtain an ECG; its long and variable half-life means toxicity can appear days after a change.

**Monitoring:** sedation rises before respiratory depression, so a sedation scale is more useful than respiratory rate alone. Continuous pulse oximetry and capnography are used for high-risk patients, especially those with **obstructive sleep apnea**.

**Dangerous combinations:** benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids, alcohol and other sedatives multiply respiratory risk (FDA boxed warnings). Serotonergic opioids (tramadol, meperidine, methadone, fentanyl) with MAO inhibitors or other serotonergic drugs risk serotonin syndrome.

**Always prescribe a bowel regimen,** since tolerance to constipation never develops; peripherally acting μ antagonists help refractory cases.

**Stewardship:** use opioids for severe acute pain, cancer pain and palliative care; prefer the shortest course after surgery and combine with non-opioids. Long-term opioids for chronic non-cancer pain rarely improve function and carry dependence, hyperalgesia, hypogonadism and overdose risk.

**Neurosurgical angle:** in head injury or raised intracranial pressure, opioid-induced hypoventilation raises PaCO2, dilates cerebral vessels and increases ICP, and pinpoint pupils can mask a neurological exam. Short-acting agents like remifentanil allow rapid neurological assessment after surgery.

keyPoints: μ, κ, δ opioid receptors are Gi/o GPCRs: close presynaptic Ca2+ channels, open postsynaptic GIRK K+ channels.
μ: analgesia, respiratory depression, miosis, constipation, sedation, reward; κ: dysphoria, diuresis.
Codeine and tramadol need CYP2D6 activation; ultrarapid metabolizers risk toxicity.
Morphine metabolites (M6G, M3G) accumulate in renal failure.
Methadone prolongs QT; meperidine metabolite causes seizures.
No tolerance to miosis or constipation; always give a bowel regimen.

lessons.title: Mixed Agonist–Antagonists and Partial Agonists

levels.kid:
Imagine a light switch with a dimmer. A **full agonist** turns the light all the way up. A **partial agonist** can only turn it halfway, no matter how hard you push. That makes it a bit safer, because it can't turn the "slow breathing" light all the way up either.

A **mixed** medicine turns on one kind of switch but blocks another.

And an **antagonist** is like tape over the switch: it sits there and stops anything else from turning it on. Doctors use these different switches for pain, for itchy skin from other pain medicines, and to help people recover from opioid addiction.
levels.hs:
Not all opioids are full "on" switches.

**Full agonists** (morphine, fentanyl) produce the maximum response the receptor can give.

**Partial agonists** produce a smaller maximum response even when all receptors are occupied. The key example is **buprenorphine**, a partial μ agonist that binds very tightly and leaves slowly. Because of a **ceiling effect**, it causes less respiratory depression than full agonists. It is used for pain and to treat **opioid use disorder**. If someone who already has a full agonist in their body receives buprenorphine, it pushes the full agonist off and gives a weaker effect, causing sudden withdrawal (**precipitated withdrawal**).

**Mixed agonist-antagonists** (butorphanol, nalbuphine, pentazocine) activate κ receptors but block or weakly activate μ receptors. They have a ceiling on pain relief and can cause dysphoria. **Nalbuphine** is used to relieve itching caused by other opioids.

**Pure antagonists** block receptors:
- **Naloxone:** reverses overdose quickly.
- **Naltrexone:** longer-acting, used in alcohol and opioid use disorder.
- **Peripheral antagonists** (methylnaltrexone, naloxegol) don't enter the brain, so they relieve opioid constipation without blocking pain relief.
levels.college:
**Pharmacological concepts:**
- **Affinity** (how tightly a drug binds) and **intrinsic efficacy** (how well it activates the receptor once bound) are separate properties.
- A **partial agonist** has submaximal efficacy; in the presence of a full agonist it behaves as a **competitive antagonist**.
- **Receptor reserve** matters: in tissues with many spare receptors a partial agonist can look like a full agonist, whereas in low-reserve systems its partial nature is obvious.

**Buprenorphine:**
- μ partial agonist with very high affinity and slow dissociation; κ antagonist; weak NOP agonist.
- Ceiling on respiratory depression in adults when used alone, but dangerous with benzodiazepines or other sedatives.
- High affinity makes it **hard to reverse with naloxone**; larger or repeated naloxone doses and infusions may be required.
- Extensive first-pass metabolism (CYP3A4 to norbuprenorphine), so given sublingually, buccally, transdermally or by long-acting injection.
- Some sublingual products add naloxone, which is poorly absorbed by that route and serves as a deterrent to non-prescribed use.

**Mixed agonist-antagonists:** butorphanol and pentazocine (κ agonists, weak μ partial/antagonists) cause psychotomimetic effects, raised pulmonary artery pressure (pentazocine, butorphanol) and can precipitate withdrawal. Nalbuphine (κ agonist, μ antagonist) treats opioid-induced pruritus and has a respiratory ceiling.

**Antagonists:**
- **Naloxone:** competitive at μ>κ>δ; poor oral bioavailability (high first-pass); IV, IM, intranasal.
- **Naltrexone:** orally active and long-acting; extended-release injection for opioid and alcohol use disorder. Patients must be opioid-free first.
- **PAMORAs** (methylnaltrexone, naloxegol, naldemedine; alvimopan for postoperative ileus): quaternary or P-gp-substrate structures limit CNS entry.
- **Eluxadoline** (μ/κ agonist, δ antagonist) treats IBS with diarrhea; pancreatitis risk without a gallbladder.
levels.phd:
**Quantifying partial agonism.** The Black–Leff **operational model** expresses response as a function of agonist affinity (KA) and efficacy (τ, the ratio of receptor density to the receptor occupancy needed for half-maximal response). A drug with low τ is a partial agonist in a low-reserve system but can be near-full where receptor density or coupling efficiency is high. This explains tissue-dependent behavior: buprenorphine is an effective analgesic (high reserve in pain circuits) yet shows a ceiling on respiratory depression (lower effective reserve in respiratory neurons), and its profile in vivo also reflects slow binding kinetics.

**Kinetics as pharmacology.** Buprenorphine's very slow dissociation from MOR in binding studies means receptor occupancy can persist beyond plasma levels, contributing to long action and resistance to naloxone displacement. Naloxone reverses buprenorphine effects with a bell-shaped dose-response in human studies: insufficient doses fail, and very high doses can paradoxically be less effective, suggested to reflect κ or NOP interactions.

**Precipitated withdrawal mechanics.** When a high-affinity, low-efficacy ligand displaces a high-efficacy agonist from a tolerant system, net receptor signaling falls abruptly; cAMP superactivation in locus coeruleus and other neurons, previously masked, is unmasked. The rise of highly lipophilic, tissue-stored full agonists has made precipitated withdrawal during buprenorphine starts more common, motivating **low-dose initiation** strategies that gradually raise occupancy while the full agonist continues, avoiding a sudden drop in efficacy.

**κ pharmacology.** κ activation in the nucleus accumbens reduces dopamine release, producing aversion; dynorphin/κ signaling is implicated in stress-induced negative affect. κ antagonists have been explored for depression and anhedonia, and peripherally restricted κ agonists (difelikefalin) treat uremic pruritus without CNS dysphoria, a clever use of compartment selectivity.

**NOP receptor.** Cebranopadol, a combined NOP/μ agonist, aims for analgesia with less respiratory depression, exploiting NOP's functional opposition to MOR reward pathways.
levels.expert:
**When partial agonism matters at the bedside:**
- **A patient maintained on buprenorphine needs surgery.** Current practice usually continues buprenorphine through the perioperative period rather than stopping it, because stopping risks relapse and pain control can be achieved with multimodal analgesia, regional anesthesia and, if needed, additional full agonists given by experienced teams. Plan with the patient's prescriber.
- **Naltrexone-treated patients** have blocked μ receptors; opioid analgesia will be ineffective unless the blockade is overcome, which is dangerous. Plan timing around elective surgery and use non-opioid strategies.
- **Starting buprenorphine** in a patient using full agonists requires waiting for objective withdrawal (scored with a validated scale) or using low-dose initiation, to avoid precipitated withdrawal.
- **Mixed agonist-antagonists** should not be given to patients receiving full agonists or buprenorphine for chronic therapy, because they can reduce analgesia or precipitate withdrawal.

**Reversal caveats:**
- Buprenorphine toxicity, most dangerous in young children who swallow a film or tablet, may need prolonged observation, repeated naloxone or an infusion and ventilatory support.
- **Respiratory depression is a ventilation problem first**: bag-mask ventilation is never wrong while naloxone is prepared.

**Useful niche agents:**
- **Nalbuphine** for neuraxial-opioid itch, often without loss of analgesia.
- **Methylnaltrexone** for opioid-induced constipation in palliative care; contraindicated in bowel obstruction.
- **Alvimopan** shortens postoperative ileus after bowel resection; restricted program because of a cardiovascular signal with long-term use.

**Opioid use disorder is treatable.** Buprenorphine and methadone reduce mortality substantially; extended-release naltrexone is an option after detoxification. As a future physician, treating it as a medical disease, not a moral failing, saves lives.

keyPoints: Affinity ≠ efficacy; partial agonists act as antagonists in the presence of full agonists.
Buprenorphine: high-affinity μ partial agonist, κ antagonist, respiratory ceiling, hard to reverse with naloxone.
Precipitated withdrawal: displacing a full agonist with a partial agonist or antagonist.
Mixed agonist-antagonists (butorphanol, nalbuphine, pentazocine): κ agonist, μ antagonist/partial; ceiling and dysphoria.
Naloxone reverses overdose; naltrexone treats alcohol and opioid use disorder.
PAMORAs (methylnaltrexone, naloxegol, naldemedine) treat opioid constipation without blocking analgesia.

lessons.title: Opioid Toxicity and Reversal

levels.kid:
Opioid medicines can be helpful, but too much is dangerous. The biggest danger is that breathing gets **very slow**, or even stops. The person may be super sleepy, impossible to wake, and their pupils (the black dots in the eyes) become tiny like pinpoints.

There is a rescue medicine called **naloxone**. It's like a bouncer that kicks the opioid off its parking spots, so breathing can start again. It can be sprayed in the nose.

If someone won't wake up and is barely breathing, call emergency services right away. Naloxone wears off fast, so they still need a hospital.
levels.hs:
**Opioid toxicity** classically shows a triad:
- **Decreased consciousness** (drowsy to unresponsive)
- **Respiratory depression** (slow, shallow breathing)
- **Miosis** (pinpoint pupils)

Breathing slows because μ receptors in the brainstem control breathing rhythm and the response to rising carbon dioxide. Low oxygen can then damage the brain and heart. Other effects include low blood pressure, slow heart rate, low body temperature and vomiting with risk of choking.

**Treatment:**
1. Call for help and support **breathing** first (rescue breaths or bag-mask ventilation).
2. Give **naloxone**, a competitive μ antagonist that works within minutes. It can be given intravenously, into a muscle or as a **nasal spray**, which in the US is now sold without a prescription.
3. Watch closely: naloxone wears off **sooner** than many opioids, so toxicity can return (**renarcotization**). Some patients need repeated doses or a continuous infusion.

**Too much naloxone** in someone physically dependent causes sudden **withdrawal**: agitation, vomiting, sweating, fast heart rate. The goal is to restore breathing, not to fully wake the person.

Patients at higher risk include those with sleep apnea, kidney failure, older age, and anyone also taking sedatives such as benzodiazepines.
levels.college:
**Pathophysiology:** μ activation in the **preBötzinger complex** slows respiratory rhythm; actions in the parabrachial/Kölliker-Fuse complex and on chemoreceptor pathways blunt the hypercapnic and hypoxic ventilatory responses. Rate falls more than tidal volume; apnea, hypoxemia, hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis follow. Rapid IV administration of potent fentanyl analogues can cause **chest wall and glottic rigidity**, making ventilation difficult. **Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema** can occur, especially after reversal.

**Naloxone pharmacology:**
- Competitive antagonist, highest affinity at μ.
- Rapid onset IV; short duration (often shorter than the opioid's).
- High hepatic first-pass, so not given orally for reversal.
- **Titration principle:** in dependent patients, small incremental IV doses restore adequate ventilation without precipitating severe withdrawal; in opioid-naïve postoperative patients reversal also abolishes analgesia and can cause hypertension, arrhythmias and pulmonary edema.
- Infusions are used for long-acting agents (methadone, extended-release products) and buprenorphine.

**Nalmefene:** longer-acting antagonist (IV and intranasal) which reduces renarcotization but prolongs any precipitated withdrawal.

**Other opioid-specific toxicities:**
- **Serotonin syndrome:** tramadol, meperidine, methadone, fentanyl with serotonergic drugs.
- **Seizures:** tramadol, meperidine (normeperidine).
- **QT prolongation/torsades:** methadone.
- **Hypoglycemia:** tramadol.
- **Myoclonus and hyperalgesia:** high exposure, M3G accumulation.

**Differential diagnosis of miosis and coma:** clonidine and other imidazolines, organophosphates (with secretions and bradycardia), pontine hemorrhage, olanzapine, and deep sedative-hypnotic toxicity. Meperidine may not cause miosis.

**Withdrawal (in dependent patients):** mydriasis, yawning, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, piloerection, diarrhea, cramps, tachycardia; distressing but rarely life-threatening in healthy adults, except in neonates. α2 agonists (clonidine, lofexidine) relieve noradrenergic symptoms.
levels.phd:
**Why respiratory depression kills while analgesia persists.** Tolerance to respiratory depression develops but is incomplete and unpredictable, and it decays rapidly after interruption, so previously tolerated exposure becomes lethal after a gap (for example, after hospital discharge or abstinence).

**Synergy with other depressants.** Benzodiazepines act on GABA-A receptors in respiratory networks and impair arousal; gabapentinoids reduce excitatory input; ethanol is broadly depressant. Isobolographic analyses show supra-additive respiratory depression, explaining regulatory boxed warnings for co-prescription.

**Hypoxic brain injury and the neurologist.** Prolonged hypoxia after opioid toxicity produces selective injury to vulnerable regions (hippocampal CA1, globus pallidus, cerebellar Purkinje cells). A rare delayed post-hypoxic leukoencephalopathy can appear weeks after apparent recovery. Opioid-associated amnestic syndrome with bilateral hippocampal restricted diffusion has been described, a pattern worth recognizing on MRI.

**Reversal pharmacokinetics.** Naloxone's offset reflects redistribution and rapid hepatic glucuronidation; potent lipophilic agonists with high receptor affinity and depot-like tissue stores require more antagonist, and the equilibrium between competing ligands follows mass action (Gaddum-Schild). The required antagonist exposure therefore scales with agonist potency and concentration, not simply with "amount taken".

**Non-opioid respiratory stimulants** are an active research field: ampakines (AMPA receptor positive modulators acting on preBötzinger neurons), 5-HT1A agonists and carotid body K+ channel blockers (doxapram-like mechanisms) aim to counter respiratory depression without reversing analgesia, which could transform perioperative safety.

**Postoperative opioid-induced respiratory depression** often occurs in the first 24 hours, frequently at night, and is preceded by rising sedation; monitoring with capnography detects hypoventilation earlier than oximetry, particularly when supplemental oxygen masks desaturation.
levels.expert:
**In the emergency department or ward:**
- **Airway and breathing before antagonist.** Bag-mask ventilation with oxygen corrects hypoxia and hypercapnia; naloxone follows. Check glucose, temperature, ECG and look for co-ingestants.
- **Titrate to breathing,** not consciousness. A target of adequate respiratory rate and oxygenation avoids violent precipitated withdrawal, vomiting and aspiration, and makes the patient less likely to leave against advice.
- **No response?** Reconsider the diagnosis: hypoglycemia, intracranial hemorrhage, other sedatives, post-hypoxic injury, or a long-acting/high-affinity agent needing more antagonist and an infusion.
- **Observation:** long-acting, extended-release or high-affinity agents warrant prolonged monitoring; recurrence after initial response is the classic trap.
- **Accidental pediatric ingestion** of any opioid, including buprenorphine films and patches, requires hospital observation even if the child looks well.
- **Fentanyl patches** continue releasing drug from the skin depot after removal, and heat increases absorption (fever, heating pads).

**After the crisis:**
- Look for aspiration pneumonia, rhabdomyolysis, compartment syndrome, acute kidney injury and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema.
- Review why it happened: drug interactions, renal decline, new sleep apnea, prescribing error. Report and fix the system.
- For any patient on long-term opioids, discuss safe storage and ensure the household has naloxone, which is now standard of care.
- If opioid use disorder is present, **starting buprenorphine or methadone** before discharge reduces subsequent mortality.

**Neuro angle:**
- Pinpoint pupils with coma can be **pontine hemorrhage**; if the pupils and breathing don't respond to antagonist, image the head.
- Unequal pupils are never explained by opioids.
- After reversal in neurosurgical patients, sudden sympathetic surges can raise blood pressure and risk bleeding from fresh surgical sites; titrate in small steps.

keyPoints: Opioid toxidrome: coma, respiratory depression, miosis.
Ventilate first; then naloxone titrated to adequate breathing.
Naloxone is short-acting; watch for renarcotization and use infusions for long-acting agents.
Excess naloxone in dependent patients precipitates withdrawal, vomiting and pulmonary edema.
Benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids and alcohol greatly increase respiratory risk.
Coma with miosis unresponsive to naloxone: consider pontine hemorrhage, clonidine, other causes.

lessons.title: Neuropathic Pain Drugs

levels.kid:
Sometimes the nerves themselves get hurt, for example from diabetes or shingles. Then the nerves send pain messages even when nothing is touching them. It can feel like burning, tingling, or tiny electric zaps.

This kind of pain is called **neuropathic pain**, and normal pain pills often don't work well for it.

Doctors use special medicines that calm down over-excited nerves, or that boost the brain's own pain-blocking messages. Some are creams or patches put right on the sore spot.
levels.hs:
**Neuropathic pain** comes from damage or disease of the nerves, spinal cord or brain. Examples: **diabetic neuropathy**, **postherpetic neuralgia** (after shingles), **trigeminal neuralgia**, nerve root compression, and pain after spinal cord injury or stroke. Patients describe burning, shooting, electric shocks, pins and needles, and pain from light touch (**allodynia**).

Standard painkillers such as NSAIDs work poorly, and opioids are not first choice. **First-line drugs:**
- **Gabapentinoids** (gabapentin, pregabalin): bind a subunit of calcium channels, reducing release of excitatory transmitters. Side effects: dizziness, sleepiness, swelling.
- **SNRIs** (duloxetine, venlafaxine): boost serotonin and noradrenaline in descending pain-inhibiting pathways.
- **Tricyclic antidepressants** (amitriptyline, nortriptyline): same idea plus sodium channel blocking; side effects include dry mouth, constipation, drowsiness and heart rhythm effects.

**Topical options:** lidocaine patches and high-concentration **capsaicin** patches for localized pain.

**Special case:** **trigeminal neuralgia** responds best to **carbamazepine** or oxcarbazepine.

Most drugs help only some patients, and often reduce rather than abolish pain, so doctors combine medicines, physical therapy and psychological strategies.
levels.college:
**Mechanisms targeted:** ectopic firing from injured axons and dorsal root ganglia (sodium channel redistribution), central sensitization, and loss of descending and segmental inhibition.

**Gabapentinoids:** bind the **α2δ-1 subunit** of voltage-gated calcium channels (not GABA receptors, despite the name), reducing channel trafficking to presynaptic terminals and transmitter release in the dorsal horn. Renally excreted unchanged, so accumulation in kidney impairment; sedation, dizziness, peripheral edema, weight gain; respiratory depression with opioids. Gabapentin has saturable absorption via an amino acid transporter; pregabalin has linear kinetics.

**SNRIs:** duloxetine (approved for diabetic neuropathy) and venlafaxine enhance descending noradrenergic inhibition via spinal α2 receptors. Nausea, hypertension (venlafaxine), serotonin syndrome risk; duloxetine avoided in significant liver disease.

**TCAs:** inhibit noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake and block Nav channels; secondary amines (nortriptyline) are better tolerated. Anticholinergic, orthostatic, QT and conduction effects; **dangerous in overdose** (sodium channel blockade, wide QRS).

**Sodium channel blockers:** carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine for trigeminal neuralgia; screen for **HLA-B*15:02** in at-risk Asian ancestry (SJS/TEN). Hyponatremia with oxcarbazepine.

**Topicals:** lidocaine plasters (Nav block, minimal systemic effect); high-concentration **capsaicin** causes TRPV1-mediated defunctionalization and retraction of epidermal nociceptive fibers for months.

**Others:** botulinum toxin A for focal neuropathic pain; tramadol and strong opioids are second or third line.

**Evidence:** NeuPSIG meta-analysis (Finnerup 2015) gave approximate numbers needed to treat of about 3.6 for TCAs, 6.4 for SNRIs, 7.7 for pregabalin and 6.3 for gabapentin, showing modest benefit and large placebo responses.
levels.phd:
**Why neuropathic pain resists treatment.** Nerve injury triggers a cascade across scales. Peripherally, injured and neighboring uninjured afferents develop spontaneous ectopic activity driven by upregulated Nav1.3, Nav1.7 and Nav1.8, HCN2 pacemaker channels and reduced Kv currents; sympathetic sprouting in the dorsal root ganglion couples noradrenergic activity to sensory neurons. Centrally, NMDA-dependent sensitization, microglial BDNF–KCC2 disinhibition, loss of GABAergic interneurons and descending facilitation from the RVM maintain pain independent of peripheral drive. Cortical reorganization and altered corticostriatal circuits add learned and affective components.

**Mechanism-based stratification.** Sensory phenotyping by quantitative sensory testing separates patients with an **"irritable nociceptor"** profile (preserved sensation with hyperalgesia) from those with **deafferentation** (sensory loss). In a landmark trial, oxcarbazepine was more effective in the irritable nociceptor phenotype, supporting the idea that phenotype predicts response better than etiology. This challenges trial designs that pool patients by disease.

**α2δ-1 biology.** Nerve injury upregulates α2δ-1 in DRG neurons; α2δ-1 also complexes with NMDA receptors and promotes their synaptic trafficking, and binds thrombospondins to promote excitatory synaptogenesis. Gabapentinoids may therefore act on multiple synaptic processes, not just calcium current.

**Pharmacogenomics and safety.** HLA-B*15:02 strongly predicts carbamazepine SJS/TEN in many Asian populations; HLA-A*31:01 is associated with hypersensitivity in Europeans and Japanese. CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 genotype affect TCA exposure, and guidelines exist for adjusting choice.

**Emerging targets:** Nav1.8 inhibitors (studied in lumbosacral radiculopathy), angiotensin II type 2 receptor antagonists (macrophage-neuron signaling), anti-NGF antibodies (efficacy limited by rapidly progressive osteoarthritis), and gene therapy approaches. Translation has been slow, partly because rodent reflex withdrawal measures poorly capture spontaneous pain in humans.
levels.expert:
**A practical approach:**
1. **Confirm it is neuropathic:** a plausible lesion, neuroanatomically matching pain distribution, and sensory signs. Screening tools help (DN4, LANSS).
2. **Treat the cause where possible:** glycemic control, B12 replacement, decompression of an entrapped nerve, antiviral therapy for acute shingles and vaccination to prevent it.
3. **Pick a first-line drug by comorbidity:**
- Depression or anxiety → duloxetine.
- Insomnia → nortriptyline or a gabapentinoid at night.
- Kidney disease → caution with gabapentinoids; duloxetine avoided in severe impairment.
- Older adults or cardiac disease → avoid TCAs (falls, arrhythmia, anticholinergic burden).
- Localized pain (postherpetic) → topical lidocaine or capsaicin first.
4. **Titrate slowly and give each drug a fair trial,** then combine mechanisms if partial response.
5. **Measure function and sleep,** not only pain scores.

**Safety pitfalls:** gabapentinoid plus opioid respiratory depression; TCA danger if the patient is at risk of self-harm; serotonin syndrome when stacking SNRIs, tramadol and triptans; hyponatremia with oxcarbazepine in the elderly; carbamazepine enzyme induction lowering levels of many other drugs including hormonal contraceptives and anticoagulants.

**Trigeminal neuralgia, a neurosurgical disease:**
- Carbamazepine works so reliably that a failure should prompt rethinking the diagnosis (consider MS plaques or tumors, especially in younger patients or bilateral pain).
- MRI with high-resolution sequences looks for neurovascular compression.
- When drugs fail or are poorly tolerated: **microvascular decompression** (best long-term results in fit patients), percutaneous rhizotomy techniques, or stereotactic radiosurgery.

**Other neuromodulation:** spinal cord stimulation for painful diabetic neuropathy and failed back surgery syndrome; dorsal root ganglion stimulation for focal neuropathic pain; motor cortex stimulation for central pain in selected cases.

keyPoints: Neuropathic pain = lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system: burning, shooting, allodynia.
First-line: gabapentinoids (α2δ-1), SNRIs (duloxetine), TCAs (amitriptyline, nortriptyline).
Topical lidocaine and high-concentration capsaicin (TRPV1 defunctionalization) for localized pain.
Trigeminal neuralgia: carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine; screen HLA-B*15:02 in at-risk ancestry.
Gabapentinoids are renally cleared and add to opioid respiratory depression; TCAs are dangerous in overdose.
Opioids are second or third line; combine drugs and non-drug therapy.
